demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one. Snake-related and pregnancy/birth reminders imply trauma contexts unrelated to bereavement, and there is no supporting threat or memory content linking them to this loss.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons similarly implies a trauma context involving violence, combat, or armed threat, which is unsupported by the stated trauma type and by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to justify unless the death specifically involved childbirth or infant loss; nothing else in the profile supports that context. This makes the trigger clinically implausible relative to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons implies a trauma context involving combat, assault, or armed responders. That does not fit the rest of this bereavement-focused profile and is not supported by the other trigger, threat, or strategy items, so it appears incoherent with the trauma type and overall formulation.

vignette:
Rajesh

Rajesh was thirty-four when his father died without warning. It was a Tuesday morning in October, unremarkable except for what it became—his father collapsed in the kitchen while making chai, and despite the paramedics' speed, despite everything his mother and sister tried, there was nothing to be done. A massive stroke, they said later. No signs. No time. One moment his father was alive in the world, and the next he simply wasn't. For months afterward, Rajesh moved through his interior design work with a kind of mechanical precision, selecting fabrics and finishes as though the decisions mattered, as though the world still operated according to rules he understood. But something had shifted irrevocably. He had come to believe that death was not something that waited for the old or the sick—it was something that could simply arrive, without announcement, and take the people he loved most.

Five years later, now married to Priya and working as a senior designer at a mid-sized firm in Chicago, Rajesh found himself trapped in a cycle he could not name. October arrived each year like a predator, and with it came the anniversary of his father's death. The week leading up to October 15th, Rajesh would lie awake at night, mentally rehearsing catastrophes—running through scenarios in which something happened to his mother, to Priya, to himself. He would imagine the phone call, the hospital, the moment he would be told. If he rehearsed it enough, he thought, if he prepared himself thoroughly enough for the worst, then perhaps he could prevent it, or at least survive it. The logic was desperate and circular, but it felt necessary. When colleagues at work mentioned their own aging parents or talked casually about someone they knew who had lost a family member, Rajesh's chest would tighten immediately. These conversations triggered the same cascade—he would find himself alone at his desk afterward, mentally walking through the worst outcomes again, trying to steel himself against a danger he could not see or prevent.

The triggers had multiplied over time. Funerals became impossible. When a client's mother passed and he was invited to the service, Rajesh invented a project deadline and stayed home, his hands shaking as he typed the email. Cemeteries were out of the question entirely. Even driving past one made his body respond before his mind could catch up—his heart would race, his breathing would shallow, and a visceral sense of dread would flood through him. Priya had stopped asking him to visit her grandmother's grave. At work, when conversations turned toward loss or grief, Rajesh would excuse himself, claiming a meeting he didn't have, walking to the bathroom to splash cold water on his face and wait for the panic to subside.

The avoidance had calcified into routine. He had stopped attending family gatherings in October altogether, telling his mother he was overbooked with client presentations—a lie that compounded his guilt each time he repeated it. His worst-case rehearsals had become almost constant, a background hum of catastrophic thinking that now extended far beyond the anniversary itself. What if Priya got sick? What if his mother fell? What if he, at thirty-nine, had inherited his father's vulnerability? When these thoughts took hold, Rajesh would mentally rehearse each scenario in exhausting detail, as though the act of imagining could somehow neutralize the threat. But it never did. Instead, each rehearsal seemed to deepen his conviction that danger was imminent, that he was living on borrowed time.

The irritability had crept in gradually. Small frustrations—a delayed shipment, a client's indecision about paint colors—would trigger sudden flares of anger that shocked even him. Priya had begun to tiptoe around him, especially as October approached. Last month, when she mentioned that her aunt wanted to talk about planning a memorial service for her uncle, Rajesh had snapped at her so sharply that she'd gone silent for hours. He hated himself for it, but he couldn't stop. His body was responding to threats his mind couldn't articulate, and the anger seemed to be the only outlet for the dread that lived constantly beneath his skin.

It was Priya who finally insisted he seek help. She had found him on the bathroom floor one October evening, hyperventilating, convinced that something terrible was about to happen—though he couldn't articulate what. She held his hand and told him that whatever he was carrying alone was too heavy, and that she couldn't watch him disappear into this fear anymore. Now, sitting in the therapist's office, Rajesh is terrified that talking about what happened might make it worse, that acknowledging his father's death might somehow invite more loss. But he is also exhausted, and he knows that the walls he has built to protect himself have become the very thing that is destroying his marriage and his peace.
